entry_state: Customer advances now preserve both monetary balances and consumed-credit history. Performance, billing, collection and replay remain separate. findings.judgment: The 100-unit return example retains the measured return estimate and its date. Moving from 10 to 12 expected returns gives revenue 880, refund liability 120, sale cost 528 and recovery asset 72. Eight final returns produce second-year profit 16 and cumulative profit 368. The displayed indirect cash bridges reconcile to 1000 and −80 without recognizing sale or cost twice.

Recovery cost 1 and deterioration 0.5 lower the 12-unit recovery asset to 54, while refund liability remains 120. Exchanges and defective replacements are distinguished from returns. The separately purchasable warranty allocates the 108 price as product 90/service 18 using 100/20 standalone prices; six supported service months earn 9.

The warranty completes with year-one profit 36, cash 105 and remaining service liability 9; the second period earns profit 6 and closes at cash/equity 102. Assurance-only coverage points to 9.4.13 rather than borrowing the service pattern. The distinct-goods modification allocates (60+48)/(6+6)=9 only to remaining units, preserving the original four deliveries' revenue 40.

The goods modification retains first-year revenue 94/profit 34 and second-year revenue 54/profit 18, with lifetime cash 148 and profit 52. The integrated promise instead uses revised cumulative revenue 130×0.30=39 and catch-up −1. Its progress measure is independently supported rather than inferred from costs. Unknown enforceability, unapproved amendments and mixed obligations retain separate dispositions.

Principal and agent cases have the same final cash/profit 20 but revenue 120 versus 20 because control and promised service differ. Cash-flow gross/net presentation remains a separate AASB 107 question. The transition to cost histories explains why customer-side receipts cannot determine inventory or equipment measurement.

The second inventory example gives FIFO cost/stock 26/24 and weighted average 30/20. Reversal is capped at original 24. Depreciation changes prospectively from the retained carrying value. Equipment preparation then separates PPE cost 120, sample production cost 6, excluded period expense 6 and sale revenue 8; no sample margin is netted against the machine.

four_ledgers.reader_comprehension: The sequence contrasts return, service, modified promise and agency obligations through their different consequences, then introduces cost memory before production. Contract facts determine which calculation applies; common cash totals do not collapse the alternatives.
four_ledgers.mathematical_integrity: The finite return, warranty, modification and inventory calculations were followed and their stated totals checked. Progress and return estimates remain supplied measurements; arithmetic does not establish their empirical adequacy.
four_ledgers.source_fidelity: The historical Australian for-profit scope and the specific AASB 15/102/116 paragraph boundaries remain visible. The service/assurance and principal/cash-presentation distinctions survive; no US or ASBE rule is inferred from these examples.
four_ledgers.typography: 119–124 were actually read in order. Displayed return and modification equations remain adjacent to their assumptions and interpretations. The split sample-production example continues onto 125 without a confirmed layout or reference defect.

exit_state: Customer-side obligations now distinguish refunds, additional service, changed distinct goods, integrated progress and agency. Cost history has moved to inventory and equipment. The machine example has recognized PPE 120, sample cost 6, excluded expense 6 and revenue 8; its balance, depreciation and cash consequences continue on 125 before broader production costs.
